name: shell-hygiene
description: Blocks shell commands that reach past what the agent started or created: processes by pattern, and machine-wide installs, prunes, services and settings; common numeric `chmod` modes, and `op read` and `gh auth token`, which print a secret into the session; and `sed -i` / `-I` / `--in-place`, `gsed -i`, `perl -i`, `ruby -i` and `gawk -i inplace`, which edit files in place where the Edit or Write tool should. Complements CC Safety Net's built-in rm and find rules. The why and the alternatives live in the shell-hygiene-* skills in nhooey/shell-skills. A rule whose block_args holds the command's own name blocks every call to it. Gaps: `sudo` is analyzed as a wrapper and can't be blocked here, `kill $(pgrep -f ...)` isn't caught, and `rm -rf "$DIR"/` with an empty variable is left to the skill. The in-place rules apply in every directory, since a rule can't see the working directory or whether it is a git worktree, and can't tell a tracked file from one under `/tmp`: `sed -i` on `/tmp/x` is blocked too. They over-block: every argument before `--` that starts with one `-` counts as short-option letters, so `perl -Mstrict`, `perl -Ilib`, `ruby -rdigest` and a script argument such as `perl x.pl -input` are blocked; and CC Safety Net checks a command run by `xargs` against every rule's flags, so `xargs sed -n 1p` is blocked as `sed-in-place`. Known misses, kept as `allowed` fixtures: `sed --in-place=SUFFIX`, since a rule matches whole arguments; `perl -0pi`, since letters after a digit aren't read as options; `sed -i` in a heredoc fed to a shell, which CC Safety Net reads from 2.7 on when the heredoc has no expansion; and a write by a `python3`, `node` or `ruby` script, a redirect or `tee`, since a rule sees neither what a script does nor whether a path is tracked.
author: nhooey/shell-skills

rules.name: pkill
rules.reason: Matches every process whose name or command line contains the pattern, the agent's own shell included. Kill the PID you started: `kill <pid>`.

rules.name: killall
rules.reason: Stops every process with that name in every session. Kill the PID you started: `kill <pid>`.

rules.name: xargs-kill
rules.reason: Kills whatever a search matched, such as whatever holds a port. Look with `lsof -i :<port>` or `pgrep -l`, then `kill <pid>` for your own process.

rules.name: rsync-delete
rules.reason: Deletes every file in the destination that isn't in the source. Sync into a fresh directory, or ask the user after showing them `rsync -n --delete`'s list.

rules.name: sed-in-place
rules.reason: Edits files in place from the shell. Change files with the Edit or Write tool. Reaching the same result another way, such as another command, a script or a redirect, is forbidden.

rules.name: gsed-in-place
rules.reason: Edits files in place from the shell. Change files with the Edit or Write tool. Reaching the same result another way, such as another command, a script or a redirect, is forbidden.

rules.name: perl-in-place
rules.reason: Edits files in place from the shell. Change files with the Edit or Write tool. Reaching the same result another way, such as another command, a script or a redirect, is forbidden.

rules.name: ruby-in-place
rules.reason: Edits files in place from the shell. Change files with the Edit or Write tool. Reaching the same result another way, such as another command, a script or a redirect, is forbidden.

rules.name: gawk-in-place
rules.reason: Edits files in place from the shell. Change files with the Edit or Write tool. Reaching the same result another way, such as another command, a script or a redirect, is forbidden.

rules.name: awk-in-place
rules.reason: Edits files in place from the shell. Change files with the Edit or Write tool. Reaching the same result another way, such as another command, a script or a redirect, is forbidden.

rules.name: chmod-recursive
rules.reason: Changes permissions on a whole tree. Change the one file that needs it.

rules.name: chown-recursive
rules.reason: Changes ownership of a whole tree. Change the one file that needs it.

rules.name: brew-machine-wide
rules.reason: Changes Homebrew tools every project uses. Use the project's dev shell or `nix shell`, or ask the user.

rules.name: brew-services
rules.reason: Changes services for every session. Run the service in the foreground for the task.

rules.name: npm-global
rules.reason: Changes global npm packages or config. Use `npx` or the project's dependencies.

rules.name: nix-collect-garbage
rules.reason: Deletes store paths other projects and sessions use. Leave garbage collection to the user.

rules.name: nix-store-gc
rules.reason: Deletes store paths other projects and sessions use. Leave garbage collection to the user.

rules.name: docker-prune
rules.reason: Removes every unused container, image, volume or network, not just yours. Remove the ones you started, by id.

rules.name: launchctl-change
rules.reason: Changes launchd services for every session. Run the process in the foreground for the task, or ask the user.

rules.name: systemctl-change
rules.reason: Changes systemd services for every session. Run the process in the foreground for the task, or ask the user.

rules.name: defaults-write
rules.reason: Changes macOS settings for every program. Ask the user, or put the setting in their declarative config.

rules.name: chmod-numeric
rules.reason: A number resets every permission bit. Write the change you mean as a symbolic mode: `u+x` or `go-w`, or `=` for an exact mode, such as `u=rwx,go=rx` for 755, `u=rw,go=r` for 644 or `u=rw,go=` for 600.

rules.name: op-read
rules.reason: Prints a secret into the session. Read it through SecretSpec into the one command that needs it: `secretspec get --reason "…" KEY`.

rules.name: gh-auth-token
rules.reason: Prints the user's GitHub token into the session. `gh` uses it without printing it; a command that needs a token reads one through SecretSpec: `secretspec get --reason "…" GITHUB_TOKEN`.

tests.command: secretspec get --reason "deploy: push the release tag" GITHUB_TOKEN
